CICO trainer

A cricothyroidotomy training manikin that breathes and bleeds, designed and built during 12 weeks of work experience.

Context
12 weeks of work experience in the lab of Dr Manish Sreenivasa, Faculty of Engineering and Information Sciences, University of Wollongong (UOW)
My role
Designer and creator of the whole manikin, working largely without oversight: mechanical design, 3D printing, silicone casting, electronics and coding
Customer
A medical practitioner working in a local hospital
Outcome
The customer has requested 10 further manikins of similar design
Key learning Overview and use case Video Design process Reflection Capabilities shown

Key learning

Skill gained
Taking a design from customer requirements to a delivered product, and learning silicone casting and ballistic gel from scratch.
Evidence
The customer assessed the manikin against the agreed requirements and requested 10 further manikins.
Next step
Add a tube from the mouth to the larynx, a neater neck cover and a convulsion function, and keep in more regular contact with the customer during these future developments.

Overview and use case

A can't intubate, can't oxygenate (CICO) emergency occurs when a patient can be neither ventilated nor given a breathing tube. The technique is a front of neck access procedure called a cricothyroidotomy. Clinicians perform it rarely, so competence depends on
simulation training.

During 12 weeks of work experience I designed and manufactured a training manikin for this procedure. The manikin allows students to practise the cricothyroidotomy on a model that breathes and bleeds, better replicating the experience of performing the procedure.

What the manikin does

The head hinges back to open the cricothyroid space to a gap of about 10 mm by 15 mm, the size reported in a published study of the anatomy. Cutting the skin releases simulated blood, first as a bleed and then as a spurt, and the opening accepts a practice tube of 6 mm outside diameter. The throat unit, silicone skin and other components can be exchanged, so different anatomy can be simulated.

The gap this fills

Commercial cricothyroidotomy trainers, such as the Decent Simulators task trainer, provide the basic mechanics and a cricothyroid area that can be cut open to insert a tube. Some simulate bleeding, but I found none that combines bleeding and breathing, nor the addition of a head that hinges back to open the cricothyroid space. Most also cannot change the neck anatomy beyond fat pads, so a condition such as a deviated trachea cannot be practised.

A healthcare worker commented that they were surprised by the amount of blood and the convulsions during a real cricothyroidotomy, and that existing trainers did not
reproduce them. Both gaps matter, because a trainee must be prepared for the conditions of a real emergency.

The customer

The customer was a medical professional working in a public hospital, and the design had to satisfy their requirements. The final design did so, and the customer has since requested 10 further manikins of similar design.

Video

Demonstration video. JavaScript is needed to display it.

What to watch: 0:12 incision, 0:15 spurting begins, 0:20 intubation.

Design process

  1. 1. Requirements

    The requirements were agreed with the customer before design began. Three requirements and one stretch goal were set. First, the head hinges back to open the cricothyroid space to a gap of about 10 mm by 15 mm, the size reported in a cadaver study (Anand et al., 2018). Second, cutting the skin makes the neck bleed and then spurt. Third, at least one abnormal anatomy can be modelled, or the components swap easily enough for one to be added. The stretch goal was a convulsion function, if time allowed.

  2. 2. Concept

    I chose mechanical solutions over electronics wherever possible, to make the manikin more reliable. A linkage between the head and the larynx opens the cricothyroid membrane as the head tips back, and a polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG) spring below the larynx gives the neck a realistic resistance. Simulated blood travels through 6 mm tubing to a silicone skin with channels that follow the blood vessels. A microcontroller programmed in Arduino code, with metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors (MOSFETs) chosen from their datasheets, can control the breathing and bleeding mechanisms. The original design intended to use a spray nozzle to replicate the spurting effect, but was ultimately rejected as it would either always be spraying, require some way to monitor when the silicone was cut, or have an external controller to activate the spray nozzle.

  3. 3. Iteration of the throat unit

    The throat unit copies the geometry of the larynx and trachea, adapted from an open source model, with a hinge, screw mounts and an air port. Over the iterations I shrank its footprint and moved the silicone mount into the larynx unit, so that the skin moves with the larynx instead of forcing it open. I changed the mount for the silicone skin from screws to clips for the user's convenience, split the trachea mount into its own part to save time and filament, and added support to the
    mounting plate where it flexed.

  4. 4. Silicone interface and skin

    The skin had to hold simulated blood while stretched tightly around the throat unit. The first two part interfaces leaked, so I redesigned the insertion nozzle, tried flexible thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU), and settled on a 3D-printed compression fitting around the 6 mm tubing, hinged clamps with a metal stiffening plate, and a clip mount. To stop blood seeping between printed layers, I printed the interface at a layer height of 0.08 mm with 20 walls. Leakage improved, though small amounts remain.

    The skin is cast from 10A silicone, with 5A and 15A tried briefly. Skins that were too thin developed holes along the blood vessels, a mould with three pouring ports trapped air bubbles, and the final mould is cast vertically with an open top. Silicone casting was the largest new challenge of the project, and I improved the leaks and dimensional errors by
    changing one thing at a time and comparing the results.

  5. 5. Testing and handover

    The customer assessed the manikin against the agreed requirements. In my own functional test, recorded on video, the first cuts bled and later cuts sprayed blood, and the opening accepted the 6 mm practice tube. The head resists flexion through the spring of the skin and the PETG spring, and the landmarks for finding the cricothyroid membrane by the laryngeal handshake technique are distinct.

    The test also showed what falls short. There is no convulsion function and no tube from the mouth to the larynx, the neck cover leaves the internal parts visible, and the blood is slightly too translucent. The rigid larynx, printed in polylactic acid (PLA), also pinches the practice tube.

Methods from the subject. Assembly modelling in Autodesk Inventor, taught in MECH203, let me test tolerances and sizes before printing. Datasheet analysis from ECTE233 guided the choice of MOSFETs that avoid thermal runaway. A linkage technique from BMEG301 helped design the head-to-larynx mechanism.

Reflection

This project made me refine my 3D modelling, 3D printing, electronics and coding skills in one device, and introduced me to silicone and ballistic gel. It was my first project of this scale, and it showed me why scheduling, communication and planning matter: printing times and casting attempts were the largest bottlenecks and had to be planned around the 12 weeks.

If I built it again, I would add the missing features: a tube from the mouth to the larynx, a neater neck cover and a convulsion function. I would also attempt to keep in more regular contact with the medical practitioner, although this was difficult due to his schedule. Improvements also could have been made to the reservoir to improve fill times.

Home · Project 2 of 3

Gesture tracking band

A wristband that estimates hand gesture and finger flexion from reflected near infrared light. This was my thesis project.

Context
Thesis project (MMMB499), final year at the University of Wollongong (UOW)
Supervision
Dr Emre Sariyildiz, who provided guidance throughout the project. The project was part of PhD student Muddasir Ahmad's research, and he chose the initial sensor hardware.
My role
Designed and built the band (electronics, circuit boards and housing), wrote the firmware and data collection software, and trained and evaluated the models
Outcome
Six gestures recognised with 83.5% mean accuracy for new users after three calibration samples per gesture. Finger flexion error for new users was 12.2% of the sensor range with 30s calibration.
Key learning Overview and use case Video Design process Reflection Capabilities shown

Key learning

Skill gained
Designing sensing hardware, firmware and a machine learning pipeline together, and testing on users the model has not seen.
Evidence
Six gestures recognised with 83.5% accuracy for new users after three calibration samples per gesture, against 16.7% by chance.
Honest finding
Finger tracking did not reach my threshold for proportional control (r of 0.8 and R² of 0.5), so near infrared finger tracking is promising but unproven.

Overview and use case

The band holds an array of 20 near infrared (NIR) light emitting diodes (LEDs) that sends light into the wrist, and an array of 10 photodiodes that measures the intensity of the light reflected back. Two techniques aim to improve the signal. Ambient subtraction removes background light, and a dual-brightness option lets each LED run at a high or low current, to stop an LED flooding its neighbouring photodiodes with light. The design process section reports how each performed.

A machine learning model then estimates the current hand gesture and the total flexion of each finger. This allows rudimentary finger tracking and supports human computer interaction. Ten able bodied participants tested the band, and the model was always tested on a participant it had not seen in training, with a short calibration for each new wearer.

Where it could be used

With further development to refine cross user and cross session accuracy, as well as the combination of other sensors, the technology could support prosthesis control. This goal was decided through conversation with my supervisor. The work is a feasibility study: no amputee took part, and the model ran on a computer rather than on the band.

Video

Demonstration video. JavaScript is needed to display it.

What to watch: 0:05 Completion of Gesture Calibration, 0:07 Beginning of live gesture recognition

Design process

  1. 1. Research and system architecture

    Published work on reflective optical sensing at the wrist guided the first design. Earlier near infrared studies reported only discrete gestures, usually tested on the same people the model had trained on. That left three gaps: continuous finger tracking, performance for users the model has not seen, and how a new user can be calibrated for. Ultrasound sensing was also reviewed, but it needs voltages of 25 V to 70 V and hardware that is hard to obtain, so I chose near infrared light, which works at low voltage and fits in a wearable. I planned to use an 850 nm LED and photodiode array on the wrist, a Teensy 4.0 microcontroller, ambient subtraction and a machine learning model.

  2. 2. Electronics and signal processing

    I changed the photodiode from the BPW34 to the OPT101, which has its amplifier on the chip, because a signal this small would pick up noise travelling about 7cm of wire to a separate amplifier. A separate 3.3V regulator was added after the microcontroller's own supply proved noisy. Across three circuit board versions I removed the 10 Hz low-pass filter, which would have made each 100 value reading take about 600 ms, and I removed the multiplexer, which only added noise as there were enough analog pins.

    Ambient subtraction takes one reading with every LED off at the start of each loop and subtracts it from each photodiode reading. The dual current circuit, found by increasing a series resistance until neighbouring photodiodes stopped flooding, was tested on one participant only during the experiment. Here, it was found to reduce gesture accuracy, however, a larger scale study performed by the PhD student suggests otherwise.

  3. 3. Housing and fit

    The housing has three main printed parts, designed in Autodesk Inventor and printed in polylactic acid (PLA): the photodiode and emitter housing, the circuit board housing and a mounting plate. I modelled the wrist as an oval from my own wrists dimensions and adjusted it until the band was comfortable. The first housing held bare BPW34 photodiodes, which were too exposed and fragile, so I moved to the OPT101 and then adjusted the sensor and emitter positions relative to the skin to improve contact. The circuit board housing first underestimated the space for wiring, and the mounting plate was traced from the underside of each board to fit its components. The band housing alone underwent 15 iterations to alter design, fit and tolerances.

  4. 4. Data collection and models

    Ten able bodied participants wore the band while a script I wrote paired each reading with a label. For gestures, they repeated six gestures (relaxed, fist, thumbs up, open, pinch and point) in random order. For fingers, they flexed and extended freely for 10 minutes while wearing a modified LucidVR glove, which measures each finger from 0 to 1023 using a spring loaded string and a potentiometer, approximating the change in length of the extensor digitorum or the extensor pollicis brevis. The glove measures only the total flexion of each finger, not individual joints. Data collection ran under the University of Wollongong's ethics approved study of the PhD student.

    I trained and compared models using PyTorch and scikit-learn. Gestures used a linear model, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a convolutional neural network (CNN). Finger tracking tested six models, and the final one averages a gradient boosting model and an MLP.

  5. 5. Testing and results

    The model was trained and tested on recordings from 10 participants, leaving each participant out of training in turn. For gestures, the MLP reached 83.5% mean accuracy on unseen participants with three calibration samples per gesture, compared with 52.4% without calibration and 16.7% by random chance. Open was recognised best (94.1%) and pinch worst (78.3%). Fist and thumbs up were confused most often, because they differ mainly in thumb extension which the finger tracking experiment showed to be difficult to accurately track.

    For fingers, the error for a seen participant was 8.3% of the range (correlation coefficient r = 0.82), but for unseen participants with 30 s of calibration it rose to 12.2% (r = 0.64), and the mean R², the share of finger movement the model explains, fell to 0.10 from 0.56. Predictions followed finger movement but not its scale, and results varied widely between participants. The unseen participant result did not reach my minimum for proportional control (r of 0.8 and R² of 0.5), so NIR finger tracking is promising but unproven. Estimating all five fingers took 31.8ms on an external PC.

Methods from the subject. Literature based needs analysis, verification by testing against a reference measurement (the sensor glove), and ethics approval and informed consent for the human participants

Reflection

The main limit is accuracy for users the model has not seen. Refining cross user accuracy or solving the amputee calibration problem, and combining with other sensors for a more holistic forearm image are the next steps before the band could drive a prosthesis. The change I would test first is a calibration method for amputees: a user missing a finger cannot supply labelled movements for it, so calibration data might come from the other hand, mirrored.

Not every hypothesis held. The CNN did not outperform simpler models, and the dual current option appeared to lower accuracy, although continued studies seem to suggest otherwise. The participant with the smallest wrists scored 22.6% without calibration, likely because the outer sensors did not touch the skin, which points to band fit as a design problem. The band design is also likely the reason the middle and ring finger were consistently predicted more accurately compared to the pinky or thumb, as the photodiodes are positioned centrally to the wrist. Another design I made spread the photodiodes further, although I did not have the hardware available to test it.

From this project, my improved skills in electronic hardware design and AI model design will likely be of great use to me in future works. Designing custom circuit boards will undoubtedly be useful to create future complex circuits, and having experience in AI model design will be useful for finding relationships in large data pools.

Pulse oximeter

A proposed update to the pulse oximeter: light sources whose brightness and algorithm adapt to the patient's measured skin tone.

Context
Team project
My role
Hardware lead, with oversight of the sponsor's conformity assessment
Regulatory class
Class IIa
Target outcome
Difference in SpO2 and heart rate error between skin tones, in percentage points
Key learning Current devices Shortcoming Proposed solution Design process Regulation Intellectual property and ethics Reflection Capabilities shown

Key learning

Skill gained
Leading hardware to a schedule and mapping the regulatory pathway for a Class IIa device.
Evidence
A hardware prototype was ready early for the software team, and each step to ARTG inclusion is mapped in Figure 3.
Limit
Each skin tone pool needs its own validation study, and a patient near a boundary between pools could be matched to the wrong curve.

Current device overview

A conventional pulse oximeter clips onto a fingertip. It typically contains a red and an infrared light emitting diode (LED) on one side and a photodiode on the other. Oxygenated and deoxygenated haemoglobin absorb the two wavelengths differently. The amount of blood in the vessels also alters the total light absorbed. The device isolates the total and pulsing component of the light at each wavelength, applies a relevant equation, and converts the ratio to peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) using a calibration curve, and interprets the change in total light as heart rate. That curve is built from measurements on volunteers, so its accuracy depends on who those volunteers were (Moon et al. (2026)).

Device shortcoming

Melanin absorbs and scatters light differently in darker skin than in lighter skin, and current devices give less accurate readings for people with darker skin. Studies have reported that patients with darker skin are about three times as likely as Caucasian patients to have occult hypoxaemia, which is low blood oxygen that the oximeter reads as normal (Ullah et al. (2025)). Missed hypoxaemia delays treatment, so this error creates an immediate need for a solution.

Proposed solution

The update
Variable brightness LED controller that changes based on skin tone. The device measures the patient's skin tone on contact, sets the LED brightness and curve to suit, and applies the algorithm calibrated for that tone.
Why
A single calibration curve is built from one participant pool, so readings are less accurate for patients outside that pool, and a fixed LED brightness limits the signal on darker skin.
Success measure
Difference in SpO2 error between lighter skinned and darker skinned participants, against a reference oximeter, in percentage points.

Design process

As hardware lead, I ran this update under design controls, the structure the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standard 13485 requires for medical device design and development. Each stage produces a record that the later stages and the regulator can check.

What I did

I led the hardware design so that a hardware prototype was available quickly for the software side of the team to use once their software development plan was complete. This allocation of resources reduced idle time during development. Through company connections, the team found a sponsor to arrange manufacture of the design. With my oversight and assistance, the sponsor led the conformity assessment, which demonstrates how the device meets the essential principles required for inclusion in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG). The intended methods to monitor and document the device's performance sit within the Sai Global quality management system (QMS).


House of Quality

A House of Quality (HOQ) converts user needs into measurable engineering targets. Each need is weighted from 1 to 5, and each relationship is scored 9, 3, 1 or 0. The column with the highest weighted score receives design effort first.

User needWeightError across skin tonesCurve match accuracyLED drive rangeSkin surface temperatureUnit cost
Accurate on all skin tones599901
Safe on the skin501390
Reads quickly331110
Low cost211309
Weighted score5655694823
Design target1 point or less between groupsCorrect pool for at least 95% of patients5 to 50 mABelow 41 °CWithin 10% of a standard clip
Conventional oximeterNot controlledOne curve onlyFixed currentNot controlledBaseline

The HOQ prioritises strong relationships over many weaker ones. Raising the LED current for darker skin improves the signal but raises skin surface temperature, so these two targets trade off, and the hardware current limit in the FMEA below sets the boundary. The design targets are values to confirm in bench testing, and the comparison row is the baseline the validation study would measure.

Failure mode and effects analysis

A failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) lists how the device could fail and scores each failure for severity (S), occurrence (O) and detection (D), each from 1 to 5. The risk priority number (RPN) is S × O × D. Controls are added until each RPN is below the action threshold of 25.

Methods from the subject. Design controls (Week 2), the House of Quality and failure mode and effects analysis (Week 3), classification and ARTG inclusion (Week 1), and intellectual property and ethics (Week 4).


Regulation and ARTG inclusion

In Australia the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) regulates medical devices, and the manufacturer is responsible for classifying each device. The updated pulse oximeter is Class IIa under Schedule 2 of the Therapeutic Goods (Medical Devices) Regulations 2002, clause 4.3, because it is intended to supply energy that is absorbed by the patient's body. The red and infrared light emitting diodes (LEDs) deliver light into the fingertip, and the update varies that output with skin tone. Class IIa is a low to medium risk class, so the manufacturer needs a conformity assessment certificate issued by the TGA, not a declaration alone.

The manufacturer first shows that the device meets the essential principles. The TGA then assesses the technical documentation, manufacturing processes, risk analysis and clinical evidence, and issues the certificate. The manufacturer makes the Australian declaration of conformity, and the sponsor applies for inclusion, pays the fees and passes a preliminary assessment, with a possible audit before the device is added to the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG). After inclusion the sponsor and manufacturer remain responsible for adverse event reporting, recalls and distribution records through the quality management system (QMS), which are kept for five years for a Class IIa device.

Source: TGA, steps to supply a device (manufacturers). Standards cited as evidence: ISO 13485 (quality management), ISO 14971 (risk management), International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) 62304 (software lifecycle), ISO 10993 (biological evaluation of the skin-contacting parts) and ISO 80601-2-61 (pulse oximeter equipment).

Intellectual property and ethics

Intellectual property (IP)

Patent. The skin tone dependent controller is the feature that could be protected. The technique has proven its utility in its ability to adjust automatically to new skin tones. Its novelty is strong as other pulse oximeters use different methods, such as the Masimo SET® pulse oximeter which uses more advanced computing on the signals output.

Copyright. Firmware and algorithm code are protected by copyright automatically from the moment they are written, with no registration in Australia, and each file would carry a copyright notice. The software is owned by our company and is licensed out to the sponsor.

Ethics

Validation across skin tones needs human research ethics approval and informed consent from every participant.

Accuracy must be reported for each skin tone group, not only as an average, so that a gap between groups stays visible.

Recorded readings are health information. Access is limited to the team and the data is anonymised. Skin tone could reveal racial or ethnic origin, which the Australian Privacy Principles treat as sensitive information, so collection needs a higher standard of consent.

Reflection

Building the hardware first let the software team start without waiting, and it taught me to plan a project around the dependencies between teams.

The proposal also has limits. Each skin tone pool needs its own comprehensive study with arterial blood as the reference, which is slow and costly, and a patient near the boundary between two pools could be matched to the wrong curve. The validation study would show whether the matched curves narrow the error gap enough to justify that cost.
